concepts.name: From Application to Instruction Execution
facts: A computation like Y = Model(X) descends from an application goal through algorithm, program, system software, and OS scheduling until hardware executes instructions and returns result Y.

The workflow begins by designing an algorithm Model with input data X, which a program expresses; system software then turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task, and the operating system schedules and deploys tasks onto hardware. Hardware executes instructions and moves data to get results, completing the computation and returning Y to the application.
Step 1: design an algorithm Model to solve a problem with input data X.
Step 2: a program expresses the algorithm.
Step 3: system software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task.
Step 4: the OS schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware; hardware executes instructions and moves data.
Step 5: computation completes and result Y is returned to the application.

concepts.name: Instruction Execution and Core Architecture
facts: A computing core has an ALU for computing, a register file for data load/store, and instruction memory for pipelining; instruction execution is the last step of computing, realized as load, compute, store.

Instruction execution loads data from RAM to the register file, computes (add, mul) among registers, and stores results from the register file back to RAM. The Intel Xeon 6980P specification illustrates how threads decide parallelism, 3.2GHz decides ALU/instruction execution speed, and 504MB cache decides data load/store speed.
Three core components: ALU, register file, instruction memory.
Load: from RAM to register file.
Compute: add, mul among registers.
Store: from register file to RAM.
Threads decide parallelism; frequency decides execution speed; cache decides load/store speed.

concepts.name: Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline
facts: The five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) overlaps data load/store time across instructions, ideally completing one instruction per cycle after the pipeline fills.

Fetch gets instructions from instruction memory/cache, Decode resolves opcode and operands, Execute uses the ALU, vector unit, load/store unit or tensor core, Memory Access loads/stores data through the cache or memory hierarchy, and Write Back updates architectural state. For N instructions and M stages, total cycles = M + N – 1, giving average throughput N/(M+N−1) instructions per cycle and per-second throughput Frequency * N/(M+N−1).
Goal: overlap time of data load/store.
IF fetches from instruction memory/cache; ID resolves opcode and operands.
EX uses ALU, vector unit, load/store unit, tensor core; MEM accesses cache/memory hierarchy; WB updates architectural state.
Perfect pipeline: one instruction completes per cycle after filling, with no bubbles.
Total Cycles = M + N – 1 for N instructions and M stages.

concepts.name: Pipeline Hazards
facts: A hazard is any condition that stalls the pipeline, producing bubbles and degraded efficiency; hazards are either data hazards (RAW, WAW, WAR) or control hazards caused by branches.

Data hazards stall due to dependencies on some data, while control hazards stall due to branch and related uncertainty. Deeper pipelines make the penalty worse, and branches create uncertainty in the instruction stream.
Any condition causing a pipeline stall is a hazard, resulting in bubbles and degraded efficiency.
Data hazards arise from data dependencies: read-after-write (RAW), write-after-write (WAW), write-after-read (WAR).
Control hazards arise from branches.
A deeper pipeline causes a worse penalty.
Branches create uncertainty in the pipeline.

concepts.name: Data Forwarding and Register Renaming
facts: Data forwarding passes results directly (e.g., from a pipeline register to an ALU input) so the consumer executes earlier, while register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies.

Forwarding enables register-to-register or register-to-ALU forwarding, letting the consumer execute earlier for fewer stalls and higher pipeline efficiency. Register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies.

concepts.name: Out-of-Order and Superscalar Execution
facts: OoO execution separates program order, execution order and commit order, while superscalar CPUs try to execute multiple instructions every cycle using a wide pipeline.

OoO execution separates the order written by the programmer, the order chosen by hardware, and the order that updates architectural state; typically the compiler finds independent instruction sets to enable OoO and reduce stall time. Superscalar needs a wide pipeline with wide fetch, wide decode, multiple execution units, multiple load/store paths, wide writeback and a multi-ported register file.
OoO separates program order (programmer), execution order (hardware) and commit order (architectural state update).
The compiler typically finds independent instruction sets to enable OoO execution, reducing pipeline stall time.
Superscalar tries to execute multiple instructions every cycle.
A wide pipeline needs wide fetch, wide decode, multiple execution units, multiple load/store paths, wide writeback and a multi-ported register file.

concepts.name: Speculative Execution and Branch Prediction
facts: Speculative execution predicts the next instructions and issues risky instructions for potentially large benefits, but wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles with a recovery penalty.

The benefit is quick completion (low latency) and keeping the deep pipeline busy (high throughput); the cost is that wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles, and the recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window. Branch prediction ranges from naïve static prediction, where the compiler finds branches that would not be taken and removes corresponding instructions, to dynamic branch prediction that learns branch behavior automatically.
Prediction for next instructions: issue risky instructions on the chance of considerable benefits.
Benefit: quick completion (low latency) and keeping the deep pipeline busy (high throughput).
Cost: wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles.
Recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window.

concepts.name: Hyper-Threading and the CPU Design Tradeoff
facts: Even OoO superscalar cores have idle slots (cache miss, branch misprediction, dependency chain), so hyper-threading introduces SMT where multiple hardware threads share one physical core.

Hyper-threading introduces simultaneous multithreading: multiple hardware threads share one physical core, each logical thread has its own architectural state, and execution units and caches are shared. The summary notes a modern CPU core spends many transistors on data forwarding, register renaming and OoO execution, with ideal scenarios being control-heavy programs, irregular data structures, and OS and runtime services.

concepts.name: Control vs. Compute: Divergent Scaling Goals
facts: CPUs scale to hundreds of heavy cores because complex tasks need control logic, while GPUs scale to thousands of light cores because their tasks have little control logic and easy data parallelism.

For the CPU, hazards occur easily, forcing microarchitectural optimizations, and control logic such as branches and dependencies incurs synchronization among cores, so it scales to hundreds of heavy cores. The GPU targets tasks that are easy to parallel with less control logic, e.g. vector processing, scaling to 1,000s–10,000s of light cores for 10x–100x the computing power of a CPU.
CPU goal: be general to complex tasks
GPU goal: be specific to tasks that are easy to parallel
CPU hazards force many microarchitecture optimizations
GPU control logic is less and data parallelism is easy, e.g. vector processing
GPU delivers 10x to 100x computing power than CPU

The warp scheduler packages a branch of threads into a warp, decides which warp runs in a time slot, shares a register file among those threads, and schedules another ready warp when one waits.

concepts.name: CUDA Programming and Execution Model
facts: CUDA maps GPU-level jobs to kernels, SM-level jobs to thread blocks, minimal executing units to warps of threads, and operators to threads, with each block assigned to one SM (up to 8 per SM).

In the VecAdd example, each thread computes its index as blockDim.x * blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x and writes C[i] = A[i] + B[i]. A thread block is assigned to one SM with up to 8 blocks per SM; a Fermi SM takes up to 1536 threads (e.g. 256*6 or 512*3 blocks), each block divides into 32-thread warps scheduled by the warp scheduler, and SIMT lets threads in a warp run different branches.

concepts.name: Control Divergence
facts: Intra-warp control divergence occurs when threads in a warp branch to different paths, so only a subset executes and SIMD pipeline utilization is wasted.

A GPU uses a SIMD pipeline to save area on control logic and groups scalar threads into warps; branch divergence arises when threads inside warps branch to different execution paths. The example shows threadIdx.x % 2 == 0 sending even threads to Do_this and the rest to Do_that, and divergence-free programming instead uses a condition such as threadIdx.x < 32 so active threads stay together.
SIMD pipeline saves area on control logic by grouping scalar threads into warps.
Branch divergence: threads inside warps branch to different execution paths.
Result: only a subset of threads execute, wasting SIMD pipeline utilization.

concepts.name: Mutexes, Barriers, and Condition Variables
facts: Mutexes serialize access to critical sections, while barriers make all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point and condition variables let a thread sleep until a condition becomes true.

study_notes.title: Control vs. Compute: Divergent Scaling Goals

required_points.text: CPUs scale to hundreds of heavy cores because complex tasks need control logic, while GPUs scale to thousands of light cores because their tasks have little control logic and easy data parallelism.

   Difference of Scaling Cores: Control vs. Compute

¡ CPU’s Goal: Be general to complex tasks.

   ¡  Hazards are easy to occur, forcing CPU microarchitecture to implement much optimizations.

   ¡  "Control logic" such as branches and dependencies in complex tasks incur many synchronization among
       cores.

   ¡  Result: Scale to hundreds of heavy cores.


¡ GPU’s Goal: Be specific to tasks that are easy to parallel.

   ¡  Control logic is less, data parallelism is easy.

   ¡  Example: vector processing.
   ¡  Result: Scale to 1,000s to 10,000s of light cores.


   ¡  10x to 100x of computing power than CPU!

required_points.text: Mutexes serialize access to critical sections, while barriers make all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point and condition variables let a thread sleep until a condition becomes true.

The mutex pattern locks before the shared update and unlocks after, so only one thread holds the mutex while others wait and the protected region is serialized; the cost is lock contention. Barriers suit phase-based algorithms, debugging, and iterative solvers, while condition variables suit worker pools and event-driven scheduling.
Mutex provides serialized access to the critical section and race avoidance for protected shared state.
Cost of mutexes: lock contention.
Barrier: all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point.
Condition variable: a thread sleeps until a condition becomes true, signaled by another thread.
